title: At Rappler summit, human rights figures call for solidarity amid AI threats
summary: 'Resistance matters, resistance can work,' Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard says

(From left to right) Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard, Norwegian Nobel Institute director Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Committee chairperson Jørgen Watne Frydnes, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa speak at Rappler’s Social Good Summit on November 21, 2026.
'Resistance matters, resistance can work,' Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard says

items: Global human rights advocates emphasized the need for collective action against the challenges posed by artificial intelligence at Rappler's Social Good Summit.
Amnesty International's Agnes Callamard and Nobel laureate Maria Ressa highlighted the importance of community support and resilience in the face of online harassment and threats to human rights.
The summit underscored the necessity for cooperation among organizations to combat technology-driven threats, with a focus on maintaining human rights and values in an increasingly AI-driven world.

MANILA, Philippines – Global human rights figures came together at Rappler’s Social Good Summit to emphasize the importance of collective action and community in fighting modern crises worsened by the threats of artificial intelligence (AI).

“Resistance matters, resistance can work,” Amnesty International spokesperson Agnes Callamard said on Saturday, November 21, when asked how to convince the public to side with human rights over profit-driven motives to the AI race.
Callamard pointed out that the public is part of a global majority willing to stand up to Big Tech.
“We must get together. Join organizations,” she added. “Collectively, we can fight back and hold the line.”
Callamard recalled how Navi Pillay, the most recent winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, faced a barrage of instant online hate after she was announced the recipient of the award.

The experience was familiar to Callamard, a former UN special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions, and fellow panelist Maria Ressa, both of whom were targets of online harassment during the Duterte administration. The two women have been vocal critics of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody drug war.

“Women were attacked in the Philippines in 2017 at least 10 times more than men. What we did is we took the attacks down. It’s a curse because you feel it, but a blessing because you have the data,” Ressa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021, said.
“We studied it. We learned how to do it, and we turned it into a system where we can help others,” she added.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa: Understand AI to defend ourselves from ‘predatory’ tech

blocks.text: The closing panel, moderated by Rappler’s head of community Pia Ranada, discussed how AI has made warfare more efficient.

“If you look around us and we look at the various conflict zones, whether we’re talking about the geographical areas where war is playing out, or a conflict zone such as the struggle over where the reaches of AI are going to be allowed and not, I think we see that there is no lack of actors or individuals with enormous courage and integrity,” Kristian Berg Harpviken, Norwegian Nobel Institute director, said.
“There is no lack of organizations that are fighting back. And in the situation we are now, I think they are just more important than ever,” he added.
Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chairperson of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said breakthroughs in fighting technology-driven threats can emerge from coalitions that set aside differences.

“What I hear is cooperation, it’s the necessity to cooperate, to lift your own perspective from your regional or local to global. And many of those campaigns that have succeeded, that did receive the Nobel Peace Prize, were campaigns that were able to take away the differences they had between them.
“Even though under our hardships, our trauma, war, terror, we continue, we continue as human beings. And that is a strength which is so inspirational,” Frydnes added.
This year’s Social Good Summit is themed “We, The Humans,” highlighting the importance of human rights, values, and community in the age of artificial intelligence. – Rappler.com
